title: Shifting Into "Rates Down"

The Case for Small Caps

As the curtains close on Chair Powell’s “There is no 2% inflation target” Jackson Hole speech and Fintwit’s very own Bill Pulte investigates the things that really matter, like “Are Crayons erasable?” and “Did Lisa Cook really commit mortgage fraud?” one thing is clear: “Small Cap Summer” is blossoming into a surprising “Rate Cut Fall”.

The Federal Funds Futures market seems assured of a September rate cut (88%), and in fact implies more than 5 cuts will happen by next September. If this gets you thinking “wow more cheap cash to buy Nvidia”, this post isn’t for you (although history indicates you’re probably right anyways).

The impending rate-cut backdrop gets me interested in Small Caps, in particular inrate-sensitive names that found themselves in the wrong place at the wrong time in 2022 and have been left-for-dead ever since. Many of these names (especially within Real Estate and Banking) have been working tirelessly to improve efficiency and optimize their balance sheets, to minimal attention.

The backdrop for Small Cap outperformance is already materializing. For the first time since 2020, the Russell 2000 is projected to marginally outpace the S&P 500’s and Nasdaq 100’s earnings growth this year, and the picture gets even rosier in 2026.

The fun isn’t constrained to Small Caps. The S&P 400 Mid Cap Index is projected to put up its strongest EPS growth since 2021 next year. Despite the improving fundamental backdrop, a “rate cut” boost from Powell’s Jackson Hole Speech, and the most impressive relative Small Cap performance last week year-to-date (the Russell is now just 3% behind the S&P 500), Small and Mid Caps continue to trade at the largest discount to Large Caps since COVID.

How could this be? The truth is most people just don’t care. The proof is in the flows.

Despite the slight reversal last week, flagship Small Cap funds continue to bleed assets at a record annual pace. Money continues to flow into the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 as more and more Small Cap finally hang up their hats.

But where one man (or pretty much the entire market at this point) sees trash, another sees treasure.

I think the earnings, rate cut, and rotational backdrop for Small Caps is favorable and I am especially interested in comeback stories that are rate sensitive and are poised to gain from dovish Fed Policy.

When trading Small Caps, half the equation isn’t just how you trade, but rather what you trade. Knowing which names are especially exposed to certain factors is paramount, and establishing baskets like Tariff Slime or Government Efficiency or Mortgages leaves you prepared to spring into action in either direction, while others are cobbling together L/S pairs or baskets at the last minute.

I think it’s time to prepare a comeback basket for rate sensitive Small Caps. Here are 5 inflecting rate cut beneficiaries I am looking at across Banks, Mortgage Origination, and Real Estate, as well as a 7.60% REIT Preferred that has caught my eye.

1. Banking

Kearny Financial

KRNY:NASDAQ

Forward P/E: 8.4x

Dividend: 6.8%

Price to Tangible Book Value: 0.67x

Reasoning: Declining Cost of Deposits

Kearny Financial is a community bank operating in the New Jersey, Brooklyn, and Staten Island areas. In 2022 Kearny found itself in a heap of trouble as rising deposit costs rapidly outgrew interest income generated from its largely fixed rate mortgage loan book (currently $4.3 Billion, 80% of the entire loan book).

It’s a story that happened to many banks. Deposits costs, up. Asset yields, up slightly. Earnings, down.

Kearny’s Net Interest Margin was squeezed from 2.96% in 2022 to just 1.82% at the end of 2024 as deposit costs soared from 0.5% to 3.96%.

Now, the tide is turning. Deposit costs are already declining and Kearny’s Net Interest Margin is beginning to rebound. Kearny also still has room for improvement on the asset side as its Mortgage Portfolio slowly matures and is refinanced at higher rates.

Still, the immediate opportunity for Kearny in 2025 and 2026 lies in deposit costs rapidly decreasing. Kearny’s own analysis indicates a 100 basis point reduction in the Federal Funds Rate boosts Net Interest Income and EVE “Economic Value of Equity” significantly.

It’s a very simple set up. Unlike megabanks like JP Morgan or Citi who can flash a giant middle finger at consumers and pay them 0%, the little guys like Kearny had to raise deposit rates significantly to prevent outflows, and now that trend is poised to reverse quickly. Kearny is essentially an interest rate trade: short floating, long fixed, that went horribly wrong from 2022 - 2024, and is about to go perfectly right. Short floating, long fixed is exactly how you want to be positioned as a regional bank to take maximum advantage of rate cuts.

Kearny is currently operating at around $0.45 in earnings a year, but a mere 50 basis points expansion in its Net Interest Margin (which seems highly attainable due to 75 basis points in impending cuts this year, and a further 50 basis points in cuts next year) could boost earnings by an additional $0.11 a quarter. If we do indeed follow the projected rate cut path, Kearny is on track to earn $0.78 - $0.82 in 2026, which represents earnings growth of nearly 75% and a Forward P/E of just 8.5x.

Given the stock is already paying a sizable dividend close to 7% and is trading at a 32% discount to Tangible Book Value, I think Kearny represents an attractive way to express a view on continued rate cuts at a rock-bottom valuation. Kearny is a clear beneficiary of falling rates - while I am not calling for it to trade at $13-$14 as it did in 2022, I certainly think it will make progress closing the gap to its Tangible Book Value of $9.77 as earnings improve and the rate cut story materializes.

Waterstone Financial

WSBF:NASDAQ

Forward P/E: 10.6x

Dividend: 4.1%

Price to Tangible Book Value: 0.80x

Reasoning: Mortgage Arm Poised to Benefit from Lower Rates

Waterstone Financial is a Wisconsin-based Regional Bank with a focus on Mortgage Originations. Waterstone is essentially a hybrid, you are getting a decent regional bank with the upwards optionality of a mortgage underwriter that kicks into overdrive when mortgage rates decline.

The current 30 year fixed mortgage rate sits a 6.64%, significantly higher than the peak of 5.50-6.00% in the early 2000s, and I think it is inevitable that mortgage rates eventually decline into the 5.00-5.50% neighborhood.

No one is poised to gain more from a mortgage rush than someone like Waterstone Financial with a powerful in-house mortgage arm. After a boom in refinancing activity in 2020 and 2021, net income from the Mortgage Origination segment swung wildly from a pre-tax profit of $20 Million to several quarterly pre-tax losses of $2-4 Million. After steady downsizing and optimization, Waterstone’s mortgage segment has finally stabilized and recently rebounded to a pre-tax profit of $1.5 Million (the highest in 4 years).

I like Waterstone because it trades like a bank, but the earnings from the Mortgage Origination segment are essentially free, unrestricted cash. Unlike most banks that generate interest income from a loan book that requires hefty regulatory capital and credit risk that can linger for years, once Waterstone sells a mortgage at a gain it can do whatever it wants with the profit, and it has a strong history of returning this cash to the shareholders.

Ever since 2017 Waterstone been a share buyback cannibal, and in recent quarters it has been taking full advantage of the fact it is trading at a discount to Tangible Book Value of $18.19 a share.

In the most recent quarter, Waterstone repurchased 508,000 shares (nearly 3% of outstanding)

During the quarter ended June 30, 2025, we repurchased approximately 508,000 shares at a cost (including the federal excise tax) of $6.5 million, or $12.80 per share. The share repurchases increased book value approximately $0.14 during the quarter ended June 30, 2025.

Can’t ask for much more on the capital management front.

Waterstone is a tiny outfit. When the inevitable “Mad Dash” for mortgage originators occurs, most people will wind up piling into the usual suspects like Rocket, UWM, Pennymac Financial Services, most of whom are already “richly” valued as this is a consensus trade.

Waterstone is a name with low credit risk, aligned insiders, excellent capital management, and a significant discount to Tangible Book Value that has flown entirely outside of everyone’s radar due to its small market cap and disguised appearance as a sleepy regional bank. As long as the company continues to repurchase sizeable quantities of shares in the low 14s, I am happy to wait, and I think if mortgage volumes get anywhere near 2021 levels and the company reports a $5 Million or $10 Million quarterly profit from its Mortgage Origination segment (remember, the market cap is just $270 Million), the discount to its Tangible Book Value of $18.19 could close rapidly. It’s a hybrid name that is already trading at a palatable, attractive valuation, and the upside optionality offered by its high operating leverage mortgage segment is something I believe the market is significantly overlooking, or more likely, simply unaware of.

OP Bancorp

OPBK:NASDAQ

Forward P/E: 7.8x

Dividend: 3.4%

Price to Tangible Book Value: 0.98x

Reasoning: Declining Cost of Deposits

I’ve harped on OP Bancorp on and on so I’ll keep this one brief.

OP Bancorp is a California based regional bank. The story is quite similar to Kearny Financial, OP found itself on the wrong end of a rates move as soaring deposit costs outpaced overall loan growth and rising asset yields.

To prevent deposits from flocking away to higher rate alternatives, OP had no choice but to raise deposits rates which substantially compressed its Net Interest Margin. Luckily, OP has a much more diversified, flexible, short duration loan book relative to peers, and it took substantial steps in 2022, 2023, and 2024 to offset the rise in deposit costs with higher asset yields. Its Net Interest Margin stabilized in the high 2s / low 3s and is already inflecting upwards, and OP itself stands to gain significantly from rate cuts paving the way to lower deposit costs.

OP’s credit quality is strong, and its high insider ownership and active capital management through heavy share repurchases at steep discounts to Tangible Book Value differentiate it from its West Coast Korean-American peers. The bank trades at an attractive discount to the overall index at just 7.8x forward earnings and a 2% discount to Tangible Book Value.

OP has an excellent, diversified loan book, and lower deposits costs are missing piece that will enable it to get back to its 2021 / 2022 earnings run rate.

Given OP’s impressive growth in 2025 year-to-date and the prospect of faster than expected rate cuts, I think the 2026 estimate is too low. Given the most recent quarter’s $0.42 in earnings, I think OP is within striking distance of $0.50 a quarter in 2026, which would put it comfortably at a $2.00 a year run rate, for a forward P/E of just 7x.

Slow and steady wins the race. OP’s steep discount to peers (and its own Tangible Book Value) make it especially attractive given the rate cut tailwinds that are about to juice its Net Interest Margin.

To sum the banks segment of this piece up, Kearny Financial, Waterstone Financial, and OP Bancorp are clear beneficiaries of a rates down environment. While much of this year has been dominated by “winners” like Customers Bancorp steamrolling the Regional Bank Index, now its time the “losers” to play catch-up. Kearny and Waterstone are two left for dead names with extreme rate “torque”, and OP Bancorp is an industry outperformer that has wisely positioned itself to benefit from a downwards move in deposit rates.

When rate cut mania inevitably kicks in and people pile into anything tangentially related to Regional Banks, you’ll want to be positioned in the most clear-cut rates down beneficiaries. With highly rate sensitive deposit costs, and mortgage optionality in the case of Waterstone Financial, it’s hard to find anyone who will win more from dovish Fed Policy than KRNY, WSBF, or OPBK.

2. Real Estate

NexPoint Residental Trust

NXRT:NYSE

Forward P/FFO: 12.3x

2027 P/FFO: 15.5x

Dividend: 6.0%

Reasoning: Pure Play Multifamily Sunbelt Operator with Significant Floating Rate Exposure

NexPoint Residential Trust is an externally managed REIT focused on mid-class multifamily properties in sunbelt area. Before we go any further, let’s address the elephant in the room: external management.

Nine times out of ten I steer away from anything externally managed. In this case, I think it’s worth considering an exception.

NexPoint Residential’s advisor, NexPoint Real Estate Advisors, has done a decent job with the company and up until 2022 NXRT was industry outperformer. Ever since the yield blowup of 2022 took a hatchet to REITs in general, NexPoint Real Estate Advisors has turned down the vast majority of advisory compensation it is owed (1.20% of assets a year), which I think is honorable. In 2023 NexPoint Advisors waived $21.7 Million of the $29 Million in advisory fees, and in 2024, $21.3 Million of the $28.2 Million in advisory fees. It’s also notable that the head of NexPoint Real Estate Advisors, James Dondero, owns 3.2 Million shares of NXRT ($108 Million).

What I like about NexPoint Residential, heading into rate cuts, is that it is structured as a pure play bet on lower rates.

Not only is 75% of its Net Operating Income from highly rate-sensitive “Real Estate Investor” driven areas such as Phoenix, AZ, Orlando, FL, Tampa FL, South Florida, Dallas, TX, and Atlanta, Georgia, its entirely floating rate borrowings are poised for significant rate relief as the cuts roll in.

Currently, NexPoint has some swaps in place that have kept Interest Expense low. Nearly all of the swaps mature by September of 2026. Initially this will lead to a jump in overall Interest Expense, which will negatively impact Funds From Operation, but overall rate cuts will benefit its unhedged borrowings, offsetting a good bit of this impact. Assuming 5 rate cuts by the end of 2026 (3 in 2025, 2 in 2026), the net impact of FFO should be - $0.72.

Modelling in the positive impact of rate cuts and the negative impact of rate swaps expiring, I arrive at 2027 FFO of $2.18, putting NXRT at a 15.5x 2027 FFO multiple, still at a discount to peers.

While this isn’t a dirt cheap multiple, NXRT’s pure play sunbelt exposure and extreme sensitivity to lower rates leads me to believe added upside is possible if the path of rate cuts is faster than implied.

In the meantime, NexPoint is biding its time by slowly repurchasing shares (222,000 last quarter at $34.29), and optimizing its portfolio through strategic property disposals and renovations. During the quarter, it completed the renovation of 555 units and leased 381 of them, achieving a 26% Return on the cash cost of the renovation. As these operations continue, Net Operating Income and occupancy should increase slowly.

The Real Estate guys simply can’t help themselves. Like an alcoholics anonymous member working as a Coors light forklift driver or a habitual gambler wincing as he sells scratchoff tickets as a CVS cashier, the Real Estate guys have been pent up and tortured for years waiting to scratch their itch - they simply can’t wait to speculate on multifamily housing with cheap bank financing to jack up the rent.

NexPoint Residential is by no means a high quality multifamily REIT, but it’s the exact type of 2022 left-for-dead roadkill I’d want my money on when “rate cuts” and “housing speculation” becomes a theme. The assets (housing) and liabilities (floating rate debt) couldn’t be more perfectly formulated to express a bet on short term rates coming down. NexPoint Residential is perhaps the flag bearer within multifamily REITs for pure rates down exposure. If you are looking for exposure to lower rates and are bullish on sunbelt housing, NexPoint Residential should certainly be on your watchlist.

Global Net Lease Preferred Series B

GNL PRB:NYSE

Price: $22.62

Dividend: $1.72

Dividend Yield: 7.6%

Reasoning: Attractive Yield From a Substantially De-Risked Issuer

Global Net Lease is (as the name would imply) a global owner of Industrial, Office, and Retail Real Estate.

The company recently divested from a large portion of its Retail Assets, significantly reducing leverage from 8.1x EBITDA to 6.6x EBITDA and generating cash for share repurchases.

While the sizeable share repurchases are unusual, I’m more interested in the preferred, which is now substantially de-risked since the company has plentiful cash liquidity and its credit rating has been recently upgraded to BB+.

Global Net Lease has 4 Preferreds:

A preferred stock is a type of equity security that mimics a blend of a stock and a bond. It pays a dividend (in GNL’s case fixed, but the dividend can sometimes be set at a spread to SOFR), and preferred holders receive their dividends before common holders, so you rank higher up on the capital structure.

In exchange for a stable, predictable dividend that is typically higher than the dividend on common stock, you have capped upside.

This is because most preferreds are issued at $25 (par), and companies retain the right to “call” (repurchase) these preferreds from you a few years after they are issued. If rates drop and the company is able to issue a new preferred at a lower rate, they’ll instantly call the preferred, so it’s really rare especially in today’s high interest rate environment to see a preferreds trading higher than $25.

I like Global Net Lease Series B at 7.60%. Due to the lower initial coupon (7.25%, $25 x 7.25% = $1.72 in annual dividends), the Series B trades at a steeper discount to par than peers. You could buy GNL-D or GNL-E at 7.78% or 7.79%, but you’re also purchasing them in the high 23s and low 24s, leaving little upside to the “call” price of $25.

On the other hand, GNL-B pays a very attractive yield of 7.60%, and if rates drop and investors are willing to accept 7.25% or even 7%, the preferred could easily trade into the $23.75 - $24.25 range.

Preferred stock is the purest form of passive income, as you get paid a stable, predictable dividend with minimal fanfare. I’m happy to stash a couple hundred GNL-B away in my Roth-IRA, while you won’t get rich quick clipping a 7.60% coupon, it’s a respectable yield from a substantially de-risked company, and given there is nearly $1.7 Billion of Common Equity (221 Million shares of GNL at $7.78), the company would have to be almost intentionally run into the ground in order for them to be unable to pay your dividend.

As always, and especially on preferreds, I think it makes a lot of sense to be precise and disciplined on your entry. Given the $1.72 dividend on GNL-B, I wouldn’t want to pay any more than $22.94, which represents a 7.50% yield.

CBL & Associates Properties

CBL:NYSE

Forward P/FFO: 4.5x

Dividend: 5.7%

Reasoning: Sizeable Floating Rate Debt Exposure

CBL Properties is an internally managed REIT specializing in mid-tier Malls and Open Air Centers. I wrote up CBL extensively here so I’ll keep this one brief.

CBL stands to benefit significantly from rate cuts given it carries nearly $950 Million in floating rate debt. 75 basis points in cuts in 2025 should provide a $7.125 Million boost (10.7%) to discretionary cash flow in 2026, enabling more firepower for CBL’s $25 Million Share Repurchase Program and the recently increased 45 cent quarterly dividend.

Despite CBL’s impressive deleveraging, portfolio optimization, share repurchases, and dividend increases since 2022, the company still trades at an immense discount to peers, which is even more surprising given just $50 Million of CBL’s $2.9 Billion in debt is recourse, meaning CBL can simply walk away from underperforming properties and return them to lenders, unlike peers like Simon who are saddled with (admittedly lower cost) senior level debt.

CBL has been on a tear recently as traders continue to front-run the rate cut good news, but I think further upside is present and that CBL should certainly be on your radar as a member of a rates down basket. It’s hard to imagine someone that benefits more from the rare intersection of red-hot junk bond demand, increased CMBS interest, and falling interest rates, than CBL.

Summary and Final Thoughts

The “Rates Down” trade is already moving. The usual Mid and Large Cap suspects, whether they’re Homebuilders, Mortgage Originators (Rocket, Pennymac Financial) or Title Insurers (Old Republic) are already up considerably in August, and I think the excitement is primed to spread to Small Caps.

I like the Banking / Real Estate / Preferred trades outlined here because all of them are highly rate sensitive, yet due to the disguised nature of the trades (Waterstone’s Disguised Mortgage Arm, Kearny’s and OP’s Rate Sensitive Liabilities, NexPoint’s Temporarily Camouflaged Floating Rate Borrowings) many of them are not yet moving in sync with the “Rates Down” squad despite being clear Rates Down beneficiaries.

I never provide “strict” sizing as I want all of you to evaluate the trades using your own analysis and decide for yourself. Currently, I have larger positions in OPBK and CBL as I have been in these trades individually from earlier in the year.

If I were approaching all of these options from an entirely clean slate, I would definitely clobber these trades into a basket with the banks relatively equally weight for perhaps two-thirds of the basket, and the REIT pref and two REITs for one-third of the basket in a 2-1-1 ratio, simply because the banks are already profitable and the preferred is safer, making them inherently less speculative positions than the REITs.

Of course, how you ultimately chose to size these trades, or if you even think they deserve to be part of your “Rates Down” basket, is entirely up to you. I just wanted to get them onto your radar.
